To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in adult patients with phenylketonurea treated early, brain concentrations of phenylalnine are about 1/5 of plasma concentrations and that during an oral load with phenylalanine, brain PHE increases less steeply and is delayed compared to the increase of plasma PHE.

plasma and brain PHE concentrations correlate significantly and that plasma/brain PHE ratios are in the same range as reported for healthy controls, suggesting that PHE is not a neurotoxic compound for adult patients with PKU.

the brain concentrations of phenyl-alanine in phenylketonuric patients are about four times as high as in healthy controls, and that the dynamics of brain phenylalanine are different from those of plasma phenylalanine, which may be of clinical importance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the dynamics of PHE in the brain and the clinical significance of this finding in adult patients with early treated phenylketonuric patients.
the dynamics of brain PHE concentrations in patients treated early for PKU and their clinical significance.
the dynamics of brain concentrations of Phe and its clinical significance in patients with phenylketonurea.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in vivo H MR spectroscopy is able to measure brain concentrations of Phe in patients with phenylketonuric type I.
the brain PHE concentrations measured by means of 1H MRS in patients with phenylketonuric type I are in the normal range.

in patients with early-treated phenylketonuric patients, the cerebral concentrations of PHE are lower than the corresponding plasma levels and that the brain is less sensitive to acute changes in plasma PHE levels than is the plasma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
brain PHE concentrations are only a fraction of plasma levels and that brain PHE is not a reliable indicator of plasma PHE concentrations.
brain concentrations of Phe in adult patients with phenylketonuric type I are in a range of normality and that the dynamics of plasma and brain concentrations are different.

the plasma/brain ratio for PHE in patients with phenylketonurea type I is higher compared with healthy controls, but that it is not possible to predict the clinical status of patients with phenylktonuria type I from their brain PHE concentrations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the plasma/brain ratio is an important factor in the pathogenesis of neurologic symptoms in patients with phenylketonuric hyperphenylalanemia.
the plasma/brain PHE ratio in patients with phenylketonuric type I is high.

in vivo 1HMRS can be used to measure brain PHE concentrations in patients with phenylketonura type I and can be employed in future studies to assess the effects of different dietary regimens on brain concentrations of Phe and its relation to neuropsychologic performance.
